name: Jamal Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the front office for the history department at the university. Mornings are room bookings, extension forms from students and chasing lecturers to sign things. Afternoons it's filing, the exam timetable and whatever the head of department forgot. The best bit is the students, especially the panicked first-years I can calm down in two minutes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's hard about it for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm still learning the student records system, and I make mistakes on the exam timetable that Grace (my supervisor) has to catch. I use the chatbot sometimes to tidy up an email, but not for anything that matters. The pay is good because it's a university with a union deal, and I lived with my mum until 25, so I've got about nine months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, that the chatbot is handy for an email and that's about it. At work we'd have a laugh about the big announcement from IT that changed nothing. Online I wouldn't bother saying much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. The university changes slowly anyway. If AI stays small, my job at the university stays mostly as it is. Maybe the exam timetable gets easier, which would honestly help me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep learning the records system properly, and maybe use the AI to check my timetable for clashes. I'd keep putting money aside every month for a flat deposit with Dev (my partner). Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, like when a storm warning turns into drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would gain most from small AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace (my supervisor), probably, because she spends hours fixing my timetable mistakes. If the tool catches clashes before she does, she gets her afternoons back. I'd be happy for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already worrying you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Dev works nights as a nurse so we barely see each other, which is a different kind of worry. Money-wise we're fine, and there are a lot of office jobs around the campus if this one ever went sour.

say: The chatbot is **handy for emails**, and that's about the size of it.
The IT team's **big announcement** changed almost nothing in our office.
think: The university **moves slowly**, so my job stays mostly the same.
A tool that catches **timetable clashes** would genuinely help me.
do: Keep learning the **student records** system properly.
Use AI to **check the exam timetable** for clashes.
Keep saving monthly for a **flat deposit** with Dev.
feel: **Calm**, a little flat, like a storm warning that turns into **drizzle**.
S0.quote: If AI stays small, my job at the university stays mostly as it is. Maybe the exam timetable gets easier, which would honestly help me.
fieldNote: He uses AI **lightly** and sees it as help with his weakest task.
His only real strain is **night shifts** keeping him apart from his partner.
Strong savings and many **campus jobs** make this world feel safe.

steps.text: Run the exam timetable through the AI checker for clashes
Keep paying into the flat deposit account each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the university should use this to give staff better work, not fewer staff. I'd post the union's statement and probably add something about students needing real people. I'd keep it polite, because I'd still want my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the front office is exactly the kind of work AI eats. Bookings, forms, answering student emails, all of that is on the list. I think they'd stop replacing people, and as the newest, I'd be at the front of the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the AI training the university offers, once a few colleagues said it was worth it. I'd ask Grace if I could take on more face-to-face work with students, like the drop-in desk. And I'd join the union's working group on AI, because I'd want a seat at that table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then more worried the longer I thought about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a colleague left and wasn't replaced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd notice the work landing on me, and I'd notice the AI covering the rest. That's when I'd start reading job adverts properly. I'd still go slowly, because I've seen people jump to new jobs that fold in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'once colleagues said it was worth it'. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've wasted time on new systems before that got dropped. The university bought a room-booking app two years ago that nobody uses now. I'd rather be second in the queue than first.

say: The university should give staff **better work**, not fewer staff.
Students still need **real people** when they're panicking about deadlines.
think: The front office is **exactly the work** AI takes first: bookings, forms, emails.
As the **newest** in the office, I'd be first in line to go.
do: Take the university's **AI training** once colleagues say it's worth it.
Ask to cover the **student drop-in desk** for more face-to-face work.
Join the union's **working group** on AI.
feel: **Uneasy** at first, then more **worried** the longer I think.
S1.quote: The front office is exactly the kind of work AI eats. Bookings, forms, answering student emails, all of that is on the list.
fieldNote: He clearly sees his job as **high exposure** and doesn't pretend otherwise.
His caution is **learned** from a dropped booking app, not fear of tech.
He mixes **personal moves** with collective ones like the union group.

steps.text: Sign up for the university's AI training course
Ask Grace for shifts on the student drop-in desk
Join the union working group on AI in offices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs emergency rules, like in a pandemic. Pay people's wages while firms change, and don't let universities just sack admin staff overnight. I'd go to the protest, definitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is gone by 2028, maybe sooner. Everything I do is thinking work on a screen, so I don't get the extra three years that Dev (his partner, a nurse) gets. Nursing is hands-on, so Dev is safer until about 2031, and even then I think patients want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the flat straight away and keep the money liquid, so we could still pay rent on Dev's wage plus savings. I'd look into healthcare assistant jobs at Dev's hospital, because that's hands-on and they're always short. And I'd go to every union meeting there was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit embarrassed, like I picked the wrong job at 22 and didn't know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It goes on hold. You don't sign a mortgage in the year your job disappears. We'd keep renting and keep the deposit money as a safety net instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dev (his partner) that the nurse is the breadwinner now, and try to make it a joke. Then I'd lie awake doing sums. Dev would say we'll work it out, and Dev would probably be right.

say: This needs **emergency rules**, like a pandemic: protect wages while firms change.
Universities shouldn't be allowed to **sack admin staff** overnight.
think: My screen-based job is **gone by 2028**, with no extra three years.
Dev's **nursing** is hands-on, so it's safer until robots arrive around **2031**.
do: Put the **flat deposit** on hold and keep it as a safety net.
Apply for **healthcare assistant** jobs at Dev's hospital.
Attend every **union meeting** and the protest.
feel: **Frightened**, and **embarrassed** that I picked the wrong job at 22.
S2.quote: Everything I do is thinking work on a screen, so I don't get the extra three years that Dev (his partner, a nurse) gets.
fieldNote: He sees the **thinking-first** order clearly and applies it to his own household.
His partner's hands-on job becomes the **household anchor**.
The **embarrassment** of choosing the wrong job runs under the fear.

steps.text: Hold the flat deposit as an emergency fund instead
Apply for healthcare assistant jobs at Dev's hospital
Join the union protest against overnight admin sackings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so let's use it. Retraining grants, a plan for every university office, no surprises. I'd be the person sharing the union's plan in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have until I'm 32. That's long enough to switch to something, but not long enough to waste a year deciding. Like I said with the fast one, Dev's hands-on work gives our house a few extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd use the AI tools at work properly, because that keeps me useful for now. In year two, I'd start a part-time course to become a healthcare assistant, or maybe an access-to-nursing course. I'd keep saving for the flat, but buy smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a way I can work with. It feels like a deadline at work, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the flat in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, a smaller one, and only if Dev's pay alone covers the mortgage. That's the rule I'd set. If it doesn't, we keep renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI tools at work if they're replacing you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because for the next four years they make me better at my job, and that keeps me employed while I train. Using AI at work isn't loyalty to the machine. It's paying rent while I train for something else.

say: Five years is a **warning**, so every office needs a **plan**.
People need **retraining grants**, with no surprises.
think: I'd have until **32**: enough time to switch, not enough to dither.
Dev's **hands-on** job gives our household a few extra years.
do: Use **AI tools** properly at work to stay useful for now.
Start a **part-time** healthcare assistant or access-to-nursing course in year two.
Buy a **smaller flat** only if Dev's pay covers the mortgage.
feel: **Worried**, but it feels like a **workable deadline**, not a disaster.
S3.quote: Using AI at work isn't loyalty to the machine. It's paying rent while I train for something else.
fieldNote: With five years he becomes **practical**: use the tool now, train on the side.
His mortgage rule shows a careful **money logic**.
He again leans on his partner's **hands-on** job as the safer income.

steps.text: Use the office AI tools daily to stay useful
Start a part-time access-to-nursing course in year two
Buy a smaller flat only if Dev's pay covers it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. I'd talk about shorter working weeks and proper training, and I'd probably sound pretty upbeat. People round the office would think I'd gone soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd be fine, as long as I start early enough. I'd be 37, with ten years of savings, and I could be a nurse by then like Dev. The robots come for hands-on work around 2039, but that's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the university job for two or three years and save hard. Then I'd start nursing training at 30, with the university's staff fee discount if they still offer it. We'd buy the flat as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. There's a small knot about being a student again at 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would being a student at 30 actually mean for you day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Placements on wards, essays, no money for a while. I've got the savings for that, which is lucky. The scary bit is being slower than the 19-year-olds on the nursing course, because I'm already the slow one in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'fine'. What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could leave it too long, which is the steady person's trap. Or nursing could change faster than they say. But I'd rather be wrong with a plan than without one.

say: Ten years is a **gift** if we use it for **shorter weeks** and training.
I'd sound **upbeat** enough that colleagues think I've gone soft.
think: With ten years of **savings**, I could become a nurse by **37**.
Robots for hands-on work around **2039** feel a long way off.
do: Keep the university job **two or three years** and save hard.
Start **nursing training** at 30 using the staff fee discount.
Buy the **flat** with Dev as planned.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a small **knot** about being a student again.
S4.quote: The scary bit is being slower than the 19-year-olds on the nursing course, because I'm already the slow one in the office.
fieldNote: A decade turns his fear into a **career plan** he can picture.
He names his own risk: **leaving it too long**.
His self-image as **the slow one** follows him into every plan.

steps.text: Save hard at the university job for three years
Start nursing training at 30 with the staff fee discount
Buy the flat with Dev on the original timeline

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to train for anything. My job's gone and I'm scrabbling for whatever's left. What would help is wages being protected while people retrain, and the hospital being allowed to take on admin staff as trainees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about our partners. Every plan I made leaned on Dev, and that's a lot to put on one person. I'd rather be wrong with a plan than without one.

headlineQuote: I'd tell Dev (his partner) that the nurse is the breadwinner now, and try to make it a joke. Then I'd lie awake doing sums.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old** junior administrator in a university history department, still learning the records system.
He uses AI **now and then** and waits for colleagues to prove a tool first.
He blames **employers** who cut instead of improving work, and backs the union.
Every plan leans on his partner Dev's **nursing** job, which robots reach later.
With ten years he plans **nursing training** at 30; with two he's alarmed.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, because his job goes with **no time** to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Hospitals taking on former admin staff as **trainees**.
